This conservative attorney and activist campaigned fiercely against ratifying the Equal Rights Amendment, and her self-published pro-Goldwater book sold or gave away over three million copies — who was she?
In Catholic theology, this intermediate afterlife state purifies souls destined for Heaven, likened to dross being burned away from gold — what is it called?
Purgatory: Religious belief of Christianity, primarily Catholicism.
This Cuban revolutionary succeeded his brother as president in 2008 and served as the country's defense minister for nearly five decades — who is he?
Raúl Castro: President of Cuba from 2008 to 2018.
Abrasive and reactionary, this right-wing populist and economic nationalist served as New Zealand's 31st prime minister from 1975 to 1984 — who was he?
Robert Muldoon: Prime Minister of New Zealand from 1975 to 1984. After a troubled childhood, Muldoon served as a corporal and sergeant in the army in the Second World War.
The second son of Libya's longtime leader, this political figure acted as de facto prime minister and was later acknowledged as his father's heir apparent despite once rejecting the role — who is he?
Saif al-Islam Gaddafi: Libyan political figure (1972–2026)
Twice Austria's chancellor, this politician served as the country's top diplomat from 2013 to 2017 before becoming his party's leader and campaigning to modernize the political system — who is he?
Born Farid Khan, this 16th-century ruler founded an empire after defeating the Mughals and made Delhi his capital, earning the title 'the Just King' — who is he?
Sher Shah Suri: Sultan of Hindustan from 1540 to 1545.
Succeeding his father David as king of ancient Israel, this biblical ruler's wealth and foreign wives allegedly introduced idolatry, sowing the seeds for the kingdom's later split. Who is he?
Solomon: Biblical monarch of ancient Israel. The successor of his father David, he is described as the penultimate ruler of all Twelve Tribes of Israel under a united Israel and Judah.
A physician trained in Hong Kong, he turned revolutionary after the Qing government rejected his 1894 reform petition, and went on to found the Republic of China and the Kuomintang. Who is he?
Sun Yat-sen: Chinese revolutionary and statesman (1866–1925)
Serving as deputy president under Nelson Mandela before succeeding him as South Africa's president in 1999, he later resigned in 2008 at his party's request — who is he?
Thabo Mbeki: President of South Africa from 1999 to 2008. As president, Mbeki had an apparent predilection for foreign policy and particularly for multilateralism.
Author of the Port Huron Statement and one of the 'Chicago Seven' defendants, this 1960s New Left activist later served in the California legislature and was once married to Jane Fonda — who is he?
Born in the Ukrainian SSR, this politician served as Russia's ambassador to Malta and Greece before becoming Governor of Saint Petersburg and eventually chairing the Federation Council — who is she?
A key figure of Chile's Nueva Canción movement, this singer-songwriter was arrested and killed in the days following the 1973 coup that overthrew President Allende — who was he?
Víctor Jara: Chilean folk singer and activist (1932–1973)

Serving four non-consecutive terms as British Prime Minister between 1868 and 1894 — more than anyone else — this Liverpool-born statesman began as a Conservative MP before becoming the face of the Liberal Party — who was he?
Born in Georgia, this Red Army officer and engineer was the eldest son of a Bolshevik revolutionary who became head of the Soviet Union — who is he?
Yakov Dzhugashvili: Red Army officer and Joseph Stalin's son (1907–1943)
An early convert to Islam and a commander at the Battle of Badr in 624, this Arab Muslim general fought in the Ridda Wars and the early conquests of Persia, Syria and North Africa — who was he?
Zubayr ibn al-Awwam: Arab Muslim military commander (594–656)
Which one below was born first?
Mikhail Lomonosov (born 1711) is the earliest of the four. One of the founders of modern geology, Lomonosov was also a poet and influenced the formation of the modern Russian literary language.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Jabir ibn Hayyan (born 721) is the earliest of the four. The c. 215 treatises that survive today mainly deal with alchemy and chemistry, magic, and Shi'ite religious philosophy.
Which of these four was founded earliest?
MUMPS (founded 1966) is the earliest of the four. It was originally developed at Massachusetts General Hospital for managing patient medical records and hospital laboratory information systems.
Which of these four has been around longest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below is best known as an astronomer?
Maria Mitchell is an astronomer. Maria Mitchell ( mə-RY-ə; August 1, 1818 – June 28, 1889) was an American astronomer, librarian, naturalist, and educator.
Which one below is best known as a mathematician?
Archimedes is a mathematician. Archimedes died during the siege of Syracuse, when he was killed by a Roman soldier despite orders that he should not be harmed.
What is the atomic number of Barium?
Barium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ba and atomic number 56.
What is the atomic number of Nickel?
Nickel is a chemical element; it has symbol Ni and atomic number 28.
In what year was Zhuge Liang born?
Zhuge Liang: After helping found Shu Han, Zhuge Liang exercised near-total authority over both civil and military affairs.
In what year was John McAfee born?
John McAfee: In 1987, he wrote the first commercial anti-virus software, founding McAfee Associates to sell his creation.
In what year was Max Planck born?
Max Planck: Max Karl Ernst Ludwig Planck (German: [ˈmaks ˈplaŋk]; 23 April 1858 – 4 October 1947) was a German theoretical physicist.
In what year did Vikram Sarabhai die?
Vikram Sarabhai: Often regarded as the "Father of Indian space program", Sarabhai was honored with Padma Bhushan in 1966 and the Padma Vibhushan (posthumously) in 1972.
In what year did Michael Faraday die?
Michael Faraday: Although Faraday received little formal education, as a self-made man, he was one of the most influential scientists in history.
In what year was Lithium discovered?
Lithium (from Ancient Greek: λίθος, líthos, 'stone') is a chemical element; it has symbol Li and atomic number 3.
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-23: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. It is a third-generation jet fighter, alongside similar Soviet aircraft such as the Su-17 "Fitter".
Which country is Dassault Falcon 900 from?
Dassault Falcon 900: France. The Dassault Falcon 900, commonly abbreviated as the F900, is a French-built corporate trijet aircraft made by Dassault Aviation.
Which country is Yakovlev MC-21 based from?
Yakovlev MC-21: Russia. The aircraft made its maiden flight on 28 May 2017 from Irkutsk.
Who is credited with discovering Livermorium?
Livermorium: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research. Livermorium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Lv and atomic number 116.
Who is credited with discovering Fentanyl?
Fentanyl: Paul Janssen. Fentanyl is a highly potent synthetic opioid of the piperidine family, used primarily as pain medication.
Who is credited with discovering Arsenic?
Arsenic: Albertus Magnus. Arsenic is a chemical element; it has the symbol As and atomic number 33.
First nominated by Ronald Reagan in 1987 and reappointed every four years until 2006, this economist ran the Federal Reserve for its second-longest tenure ever — who is he?
Alan Greenspan (born March 6, 1926) is an American economist who served as the 13th chairman of the Federal Reserve from 1987 to 2006.
Before sharing the 2010 Nobel for graphene, this Manchester physicist won an Ig Nobel for levitating a frog using its own magnetism — who is he?
Andre Geim (born 21 October 1958) is a Russian-born British physicist working in England in the School of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Manchester.
This red giant is the brightest star in the constellation Boötes and the fourth-brightest star in the entire night sky — name the star?
Arcturus is a red giant star in the northern constellation of Botes, and the brightest star in the constellation.
Born in 1655, this Italian instrument maker earned lasting fame for inventing a keyboard instrument that could play both soft and loud — who was he?
Bartolomeo Cristofori (Italian; May 4, 1655 - January 27, 1731) was an Italian maker of musical instruments famous for inventing the piano.

Thought to be the world's most abundant bird of prey in its family, with an estimated 6.7 million individuals, this opportunistic raptor is known for its angled wings and distinctive forked tail — what is it?
Black kite (Milvus migrans) is a medium-sized bird of prey in the family Accipitridae, which also includes many other diurnal raptors.
Meaning 'thunder lizard' in Greek, this sauropod dinosaur genus was described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1879 from a partial, skull-less skeleton found in Wyoming's Como Bluff — what dinosaur is it?

Brontosaurus (literally 'thunder lizard', from the Greek words bront, 'thunder', and saros, 'lizard') is a genus of herbivorous sauropod dinosaur that lived in present-day United States during the Late Jurassic period.
From starch that stores energy to the cellulose that stiffens plants and the chitin in insect shells, this biomolecule family is essentially sugars and their derivatives — what is it?
Carbohydrate is a sugar (saccharide) or a sugar derivative.

The smallest recognized dog breed in the world, this Mexican toy breed has large erect ears and a rounded skull, and its genes carry a trace of pre-Columbian indigenous American dog ancestry — which breed?

Chihuahua (dog breed) is a Mexican breed of toy dog and the smallest recognized dog breed in the world. It is primarily kept as a companion animal and is characterized by its compact size, large erect ears, and rounded skull.
Native to Africa, Arabia and India, this semi-succulent herb smells like oregano and is known by names like Spanish thyme and Mexican mint — which plant?
Coleus amboinicus is a species of semi-succulent perennial plant in the family Lamiaceae.

This interdisciplinary field, whose name combines a Latin word for 'accusation' with a Greek suffix meaning 'study of,' draws on sociology, psychology, economics, and law to examine crime and deviant behavior. What field is this?
Criminology (from Latin crimen, 'accusation', and Ancient Greek -, -logia, from logos, 'word, reason') is the interdisciplinary study of crime and deviant behaviour.
This colourless, highly volatile, sweet-smelling organic compound with formula (CH3CH2)2O was once used as a general anesthetic and remains a common laboratory solvent — what is it?
Born in German Pomerania and drawn by Franz Boas into documenting Native American languages, this anthropologist became a founding giant of American linguistics — who was he?

Edward Sapir (January 26, 1884 - February 4, 1939) was an American anthropologist-linguist, and one of the most important figures in the development of the discipline of linguistics in the United States.
This antibiotic treats everything from respiratory infections to syphilis, and as an eye ointment is routinely dabbed on newborns to ward off infection — which drug is it?
Erythromycin (sometimes abbreviated ETM in reports) is an antibiotic used for the treatment of a number of bacterial infections.

This Arabic term describes the human interpretation and practice of Islamic religious law, expanded through jurists' scholarly reasoning and expressed in the rulings they issue on questions of faith. What is this field called?
Fiqh is the term for Islamic jurisprudence. Thus, whereas sharia is considered immutable and infallible by Muslims, fiqh is considered fallible and changeable.
Testimony at Joaquín 'El Chapo' Guzmán's 2018 trial revealed suitcases stuffed with $3 million in bribes paid to this former Mexican security chief — who is he?
Genaro García Luna (born 10 July 1968) is a Mexican former government official and convicted drug trafficker.

This Russian mathematician resigned his research post in 2005 and later declared he'd quit the field entirely, disillusioned by its ethical standards, and now lives in seclusion in Saint Petersburg — who is he?
Grigori Perelman (born 13 June 1966) is a Russian mathematician and geometer who is known for his contributions to the fields of geometric analysis, Riemannian geometry, and geometric topology.
With a soft, uncalcified abdomen left dangerously exposed, this crustacean borrows empty snail shells to survive — over 800 species haul their homes around with them. What are they?
Hermit crab are anomuran decapod crustaceans of the superfamily Paguroidea that have adapted to occupy empty scavenged gastropod shells to protect their fragile abdomens.
A person with this condition is excessively and unduly worried about having a serious illness, alarmed by even the most minor symptom — what is it?

Hypochondriasis is a condition in which a person is excessively and unduly worried about having a serious illness. International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10) classifies hypochondriasis as a mental and behavioral disorder.

Native to the tropical Americas but now planted worldwide, this flowering plant genus of 49 species has one member so widely introduced it's considered an environmental weed on five continents — what genus is it?
Jacaranda is a genus of 49 species of flowering plants in the family Bignoniaceae, native to tropical and subtropical regions of the Americas while cultivated around the world.

An Alberta-raised classical liberal who earned his PhD in clinical psychology at McGill and taught at Harvard before the University of Toronto, this commentator drew huge attention in the late 2010s — who is he?
Jordan Peterson (born 12 June 1962) is a Canadian psychologist, author, and media commentator.

Born of Peranakan Chinese cuisine and beloved in Singapore and Malaysia, this spicy noodle dish swims in a rich coconut-curry soup soured with tamarind, topped with prawns or chicken — what's its name?
Laksa is a spicy noodle dish popular in Southeast Asia.

The second woman to earn a physics doctorate from the University of Vienna, this Austrian-Swedish scientist became the first female full physics professor in Germany — and was instrumental in discovering nuclear fission. Who is she?
Lise Meitner (7 November 1878 - 27 October 1968) was an Austrian and Swedish nuclear physicist who was instrumental in the discovery of nuclear fission.

Made by every living organism and responsible for much of the sour taste in fruit, this dicarboxylic food additive's salt form also serves as a key intermediate in the cell's central metabolic energy cycle — what compound is it?
Malic acid is an organic compound with the molecular formula HO2CCH(OH)CH2CO2H.
This genus of about 20 species in the Lamiaceae family readily hybridizes where different species' ranges overlap, and thrives best in wet, moist soils — what genus is it?
Mentha (from Greek mntha, Linear B mi-ta), is a genus of flowering plants in the mint family, Lamiaceae.
This Nissin Food Products founder invented instant chicken ramen and went on to create the Top Ramen and Cup Noodles brands — who is he?

Momofuku Ando (March 5, 1910 - January 5, 2007), born Go Pek-Hok (Peh-e-j: G Pek-hok; Ti-l: Go Pik-hok), was a Taiwanese-born, ethnic Chinese, Japanese inventor and businessman who founded Nissin Food Products Co., Ltd.

Nicknamed for its terrifying rate of tissue destruction, this fast-spreading bacterial infection doesn't actually consume flesh — the bacteria instead release toxins that destroy it — what is this disease called?
Necrotizing fasciitis (NF), also known as flesh-eating disease or flesh-eating bacteria, is an infection that kills the body's soft tissue.

Synthesized in 2002 at a lab near Moscow and named in 2016 for the physicist who hunted down the heaviest atoms, this synthetic element claims the highest atomic number and atomic mass of anything yet known — which is it?
Oganesson is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Og and atomic number 118.
Usually numbering four and tucked behind the thyroid, these small endocrine structures release a hormone that kicks in when blood calcium runs low — which structures?
Parathyroid gland are small endocrine glands in the neck of humans and other tetrapods.
This inflammation of the back of the throat causes a sore throat and fever, most often from a viral infection, though strep bacteria cause roughly a quarter of cases in children — name the condition?
Pharyngitis is inflammation of the back of the throat, known as the pharynx.
This radioactive, silvery-gray actinide metal with atomic number 94 forms oxides in moist air that can expand a sample by up to 70% in volume — which element?
Plutonium is a chemical element; it has symbol Pu and atomic number 94.
Discovered in 1915 and too faint to see with the naked eye, which small, dim star, orbiting its two brighter neighbors once every 550,000 years, is our closest stellar neighbor after the Sun?
Proxima Centauri is the nearest star to Earth after the Sun, located 4.25 light-years (1.3 parsecs) away in the southern constellation of Centaurus.
A canine native to the southeastern United States, intermediate in size between the coyote and gray wolf. For a century its taxonomic classification has been contentious. What is it?
Red wolf (Canis rufus) is a canine native to the southeastern United States.
She co-founded a toy giant with her husband Elliot and served as its first president, but the couple resigned in 1975 amid an SEC investigation — which inventor?
Ruth Handler (ne Mosko; November 4, 1916 - April 27, 2002) was an American business magnate and inventor.
This taxonomic order groups cephalopods distinguished by having ten arms instead of eight — what order is it?
Sepiida is an order of ten-armed cephalopods.
This plant family includes both deadly poisonous species and kitchen staples like tomatoes, potatoes, and peppers, all linked by unusually high alkaloid content — what family is it?
Solanaceae is a family of flowering plants in the order Solanales.

Harvested from the seeds of the nux-vomica tree, this bitter colorless alkaloid is infamous as a poison for rodents and birds — yet was once doled out in tiny doses to stimulate the heart and bowels. What is it?
Strychnine (-nin, US chiefly -nyne) is a highly toxic, colorless, bitter, crystalline alkaloid used as a pesticide, particularly for killing small vertebrates such as birds and rodents.
Sporting beaded antennae and a pale, soft-bodied worker caste, these decaying-wood eaters belong to the order Isoptera and are really highly derived cockroaches — what are they?
Termite are a group of eusocial insects which consume a variety of decaying plant material, generally in the form of wood, leaf litter, and soil humus.
These brightly colored Neotropical birds are known for their oversized, vividly patterned bills, and their chicks hatch completely naked with no down feathers at all — what bird is it?
Toucan are Neotropical birds in the family Ramphastidae.
Measuring under five feet long, this critically endangered porpoise is endemic to a small corner of Mexico's Baja California coast — which species?
Vaquita (v-; Phocoena sinus) is a species of porpoise endemic to the northern end of the Gulf of California in Baja California, Mexico.
The largest land-dwelling member of the weasel family, this solitary, muscular carnivore of the northern boreal forests can kill prey far larger than itself — what animal is it?
Wolverine (US also; Gulo gulo), also called the carcajou or quickhatch (from East Cree, kwiihkwahaacheew), is the largest land-dwelling member of the family Mustelidae.

Introduced to the British Isles by 1500 and known there simply as 'sycamore,' this wind-tolerant maple from Central Europe can grow to 35 metres and has turned invasive in North America and Australia — which species?
Acer pseudoplatanus: Species of maple tree. It is a large deciduous, broad-leaved tree, tolerant of wind and coastal exposure.
Launched to challenge the Boeing 747, this is the world's largest passenger airliner and the only full-length double-deck jet — which aircraft, unveiled in Toulouse in 2005?
This American economist shared the 2012 Nobel for the theory of stable allocations and "market design" — applying economic theory to real-world matching problems; who is he?
Named for a 19th-century Swedish physicist and symbolized by a letter of the Swedish alphabet, which unit of length equals one ten-billionth of a metre, handy for measuring atoms and bond lengths?
Angstrom: Unit of length. The unit is named after the Swedish physicist Anders Jonas Ångström (1814–1874).

Studying humanity's past through the recovery of artifacts and sites — including stone tools dating back 3.3 million years — this discipline sits at the crossroads of the social sciences and humanities — which field?
Archaeology: Study of human activity based on materials left behind.
Affecting roughly one in five people at some point and usually starting in childhood, this long-term itchy, red, cracked-skin condition is also simply called eczema — what's its formal name?
Atopic dermatitis: Long-term form of skin inflammation.
Named for the physicist who shared a 1903 Nobel Prize with Pierre and Marie Curie, this SI unit measures one radioactive decay event per second — which unit?
Becquerel: SI derived unit of radioactivity.

A natural cross between the pomelo and the wild mandarin, this Southeast Asian citrus is too sour to eat off the tree — but the Seville variety is exactly what British cooks prize for their breakfast preserve. What fruit is it?
Formerly called the Russian Wolfhound until 1936, this Russian sighthound breed was originally used for hunting wolves. What breed is it?
Unlike benzodiazepines, this anti-anxiety medication doesn't cause sedation or dependence, and works through serotonin 5-HT1A receptors with a delayed onset of two to four weeks — which drug?
Buspirone: Medication used to treat anxiety disorders.
The largest living rodent, this semiaquatic South American grass-grazer lives in sociable herds of 10 to 20 — sometimes up to a hundred — near rivers and ponds; what is it?
A Turkish geologist honored by academies from the US to Russia to Serbia, he received the Gustav-Steinmann-Medaille, geology's top German prize. Who is he?
Celâl Şengör: Turkish scientist, geologist. Ali Mehmet Celâl Şengör (Turkish: [ˈali ˈmehmet ˈdʒeɫal ˈʃænɟœɾ]; born 24 March 1955) is a Turkish geologist.
A sweet-smelling, colorless solvent now made as a precursor to refrigerants and Teflon, this organochloride once served as an inhaled anesthetic from the 19th century onward — what is it?
Chloroform: CHCl3, historical anaesthetic and common solvent.
This process turns blood from liquid to gel through platelet activation and fibrin formation, beginning almost instantly after a vessel is injured — what's the clotting process called?
Coagulation: Process of formation of blood clots. Coagulation, also known as clotting, is the process by which blood changes from a liquid to a gel forming a blood clot.

This physical law holds that within an isolated system, nothing is created or destroyed — only transformed, as when a stick of dynamite converts stored chemical potential into heat, sound, and motion — what law is it?
Conservation of energy: Law of physics and chemistry.
A creeping vine of the gourd family that originated across India, Nepal, and southern China, this plant comes in slicing, pickling, and seedless types — what is it?
Cucumber: Species of flowering plant with edible fruits.

This acute medical syndrome develops over hours or days and causes disturbed attention, awareness, and sometimes hallucinations — often triggered by illness, substances, or their withdrawal — what is it called?
Delirium: Severe confusion that develops quickly, and often fluctuates in intensity.
The first species humans ever domesticated — over 14,000 years ago, before farming even began — this descendant of wolves later evolved to thrive on a starchy diet. What is it?
Dog: Domesticated species of canid. The dog (Canis familiaris or Canis lupus familiaris) is a domesticated descendant of wolves.
Dubbed 'the father of immunology,' this English physician created the world's first vaccine using cowpox to fight a disease that once killed up to a fifth of city dwellers — who is he?
Native to French Polynesia but nicknamed 'devil's ivy' for staying green even in the dark, this hardy houseplant has become an invasive nuisance worldwide — what's its scientific name?

Famous for the male's song delivered while hovering 50 to 100 metres above open farmland, this streaked greyish-brown bird has been introduced to Australia, New Zealand, Canada and Hawaii — what is it?
Eurasian skylark: Species of bird. The Eurasian skylark (Alauda arvensis), commonly referred to in Europe as the lark, is a passerine bird in the lark family, Alaudidae.
Reproducing via spores rather than seeds or flowers, this group of vascular plants unfurls from coiled 'fiddleheads' into fronds and numbers over 10,000 species — what are they?
Fern: Class of vascular plants. The group includes about 10,560 known extant species.
Alongside James Watson, this English scientist co-authored the 1953 Nature paper unveiling DNA's double helix and later coined the phrase 'central dogma' — who is he?
Francis Crick: English physicist and biologist (1916–2004)

Born as an air-superiority day fighter and now, as of 2026, the world's most common military fixed-wing aircraft with over 4,600 built, this single-engine jet flies on as the 'Viper' family — which aircraft?
General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon: American multi-role fighter aircraft.
With the symbol Au and atomic number 79, this soft, dense element is so unreactive that only platinum sits below it — and it often turns up as native nuggets in riverbeds. What is it?
Gold: Chemical element with atomic number 79 (Au). Chemically, gold is a transition metal, a group 11 element, and one of the noble metals.
Combined with obstetrics as a joint medical specialty and touching on everything from family planning to pelvic reconstructive surgery, which field focuses on the female reproductive system?
Gynaecology: Medical area for women's reproductive health.

Often triggered by a preceding throat infection, this childhood autoimmune disease causes raised skin bruising, joint pain, and sometimes kidney trouble from IgA immune-complex deposits — what is it called?
Henoch–Schönlein purpura: Autoimmune vascular inflammatory disease.
Defined today as exactly 3,600 seconds, this unit of time was originally a variable measure equal to one-twelfth of the night or day in the ancient Near East — which unit?
Hour: Unit of time equal to 60 minutes.
Native to Southern Europe, the Middle East, and the Caspian region, this mint-family shrub has long been used in traditional herbal medicine as an antiseptic and cough reliever — which plant?

Hyssopus officinalis: Species of plant. Hyssopus officinalis or hyssop is a shrub in the Lamiaceae or mint family native to Southern Europe, the Middle East, and the region surrounding the Caspian Sea.
An English polymath who was also an alchemist and theologian, he shares credit with Leibniz for inventing calculus and wrote the Principia — who is he?
Part of a four-person extremist cell known for English accents, this Kuwaiti-born militant appeared in Islamic State videos before being killed in a 2015 drone strike near Raqqa — who is he?
Jihadi John: Kuwaiti-British terrorist and ISIS executioner (1988–2015)
Named for a district in Turkey's Sivas Province, which large livestock guardian breed has been exported to Africa to protect flocks from cheetahs?
Kangal Shepherd Dog: Turkish breed of dog. The Kangal Shepherd Dog or Turkish Kangal (Turkish: Kangal Çoban Köpeği) is a traditional Turkish breed of large livestock guardian dog.

Native to the tropical Americas, this flowering shrub was carried to Europe by Dutch explorers and later brought to Goa by the Portuguese, becoming a notorious invasive weed across some 50 countries — which plant?
Lantana camara: Species of plant. Lantana camara (common lantana) is a species of flowering plant in the verbena family (Verbenaceae), native to the tropics of the Americas.
This genus of bulb-grown flowering plants, prized for their large blooms, is highly toxic to cats — even though many unrelated plants borrow its common name — which genus?
Lilium: Genus of plants. Lilium ( LIL-ee-əm) is a genus of herbaceous flowering plants growing from bulbs, all with large and often prominent flowers.
Originating in 1993 and written in ANSI C, this lightweight scripting language was designed to be embedded inside other applications — which language?
Lua: Lightweight programming language. Lua is a lightweight, high-level, multi-paradigm programming language designed mainly for embedded use in applications.
Sharing joints only with the temporal bones, this is the skull's lone movable bone, hosting the lower teeth and shrinking in size since humans began farming around 10,000 BCE — what is it called?
Mandible: Lower jaw bone. The mandible hosts the lower teeth (their depth delineated by the alveolar process).
Also known as flying foxes, these 197-plus species of fruit-eating bat likely evolved in Australasia some 31 million years ago — what are they called?
Named from Greek words for 'small' and 'head,' this congenital condition involves a smaller-than-average head size and can result from genetic syndromes or prenatal toxin exposure — what is it?
Microcephaly: Condition in which the head is small due to an underdeveloped brain.
Ranging from a tiny 8-inch species to the 10-foot Komodo dragon, this reptile genus includes an extinct relative that may have grown over 20 feet long — what are they called?
Monitor lizard: Genus of reptiles. Monitor lizards are lizards in the genus Varanus, the only extant genus in the family Varanidae.

First classified by Linnaeus in 1753, this genus in the family Myrtaceae includes only two accepted species today: one native to the Mediterranean, the other to the Saharan mountains of North Africa — which genus?
Myrtus: Genus of flowering plants in the family Myrtaceae.
A former director of Russia's FSB who later served as Security Council secretary, this close Putin ally played a key role in the decisions to annex Crimea and invade Ukraine — who is he?
Nikolai Patrushev: Russian politician and security officer (born 1951)

This family of 138 primate species — including baboons, macaques, and mandrills — split off from a separate lineage of primates some 45 to 55 million years ago, yet is the closer kin to apes of the two — which family?
Old World monkey: Family of mammals. Old World monkey genera include baboons (genus Papio), red colobus (genus Piliocolobus), and macaques (genus Macaca).
A pale-blue gas with a chlorine-like pungent odour, this unstable three-atom cousin of oxygen forms by UV light and electrical discharges and shields us high in the stratosphere — what is it?
Prized wood from this fruit tree's genus, Pyrus, is a favorite material for making high-quality woodwind instruments, and China grows about three-quarters of the world's crop — which fruit?
Pear: Edible fruits from the genus Pyrus.

Combining textual criticism, literary criticism, history, and linguistics, this scholarly field traces its classical roots to the libraries of Pergamum and Alexandria in the 4th century BC — what is it?
Philology: Study of language in historical sources.
Known informally for resembling a certain dairy product due to its shape, this popular edible fungus grows wild across temperate and subtropical forests worldwide — what is its scientific name?
First prescribed in 1934, this steroid sex hormone plays a key role in the menstrual cycle, pregnancy, and embryonic development — what is it?
Progesterone: Sex hormone. Progesterone (P4) is an endogenous steroid and progestogen sex hormone involved in the menstrual cycle, pregnancy, and embryogenesis of humans and other species.
This is the name for three positive whole numbers a, b, and c satisfying a² + b² = c², like the classic set (3, 4, 5) — what is it called?
Pythagorean triple: Integer side lengths of a right triangle.
This biological process comes in two forms — asexual, as seen in cloning, and sexual, which combines gametes carrying half the usual chromosome count — what's the process called?
Reproduction: Biological process. Reproduction (or procreation or breeding) is the biological process by which new individual organisms – offspring – are produced from their parent or parents.
The second woman ever to win the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine — and the first American-born one — this physicist shared the 1977 award for developing the radioimmunoassay. Who was she?
Rosalyn Sussman Yalow: American medical physicist (1921–2011)
Arising from connective tissues like bone, cartilage, muscle and fat, this rare cancer is only about 1% of adult diagnoses but 15% of childhood ones — what is it?
Sarcoma: Cancer originating in connective tissue.
Sold as Zoloft, this SSRI antidepressant treats major depression, OCD, panic disorder, and social anxiety, with common side effects like nausea and insomnia — what is it?
Sertraline: SSRI antidepressant. It should not be used together with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs): this combination may cause serotonin syndrome, which can be life-threatening in some cases.

Headquartered in Tokyo, this Japanese multinational makes cameras, printers, scanners, and semiconductor manufacturing equipment, and sits in the Nikkei 225 index — which company?
Canon Inc.: Japanese multinational imaging corporation.

The granddaughter of L'Oréal's founder and the only child of its principal shareholder, this French heiress saw her fortune triple after her mother's 2017 death, making her the world's second-richest woman — who is she?
Françoise Bettencourt Meyers: French billionaire heiress (born 1953)

This Japanese talent agency, founded in 1962 and long dominant in idol and boy-band culture, split in 2023 into a reparations-focused firm and Starto Entertainment after its founder's abuse scandal came to light — what was it called?

Johnny & Associates: Japanese talent agency (1962–2023). Johnny & Associates, Inc. was a Japanese talent agency formed by Johnny Kitagawa in 1962, which managed groups of male idols known as Johnny's.

Spun off in 2011 to take over the consumer phone business of its parent, this Chicago-based company was bought by Google in 2012 for $12.5 billion, then became a Lenovo subsidiary in 2014 — which smartphone maker is this?
Motorola Mobility: American consumer electronics company.
Since 2003, this British luxury automaker has operated as a subsidiary of BMW, crafting ultra-premium vehicles from its Goodwood headquarters in West Sussex. What's the brand?
Rolls-Royce Motor Cars: British automobile company (1998–present)

This Japanese electronics giant takes its name from a 1939 merger and its former identity, Tokyo Shibaura Denki — which company keeps quantum cryptography on the same product list as elevators and hard drives?
Toshiba: Japanese electronics conglomerate. It was formerly also one of the biggest manufacturers of personal computers, consumer electronics, home appliances, and medical equipment.
